About These Review Renderings

These passages preserve damaged prose rather than smoothing it into false certainty. They keep OCR loss, embedded cipher tenors, and conjectural readings visible so readers can compare them against the Latin and source scan.

They should be treated as review renderings, not certified final editions.

Style C Translation: Clavis Steganographiae, Liber Primus Opening

Liber Primus

You now have, from the Malgaretic princes,^1 twelve for the diurnal [conjectured: rectors],^2 and just as many for the nocturnal ones, with their servants: [conjectured: six hundred and forty]. And note that Aroyz and Basiel^3 are always [unclear: foliugati / perhaps joined or called singly]; Misel, Barfas, Aspor, and Deilas^4 can be called two by two; the rest, however, three by three. When you wish to have three, or two, or one, take care not to err in their names. As the table teaches you, so do it, without alteration, lest you fall into danger.

Carmen Coniurationis

MALGARASador chamefo bulererin marefo bodyr Cadu mir auiel cafmyo tedy pleotyn viordi care viorba, chame ron vefy thuril vlnaey, beufey meuo chafrionty naor ernyfo, chony barmo caleuodyn barfo thubra fo.^5

Once the conjuration has been spoken, be a brave and steadfast man: those whom you have called will at once appear to you visibly. But if those called from the nocturnal ones do not come at once, do not on that account abandon your work; instead, urge them on with repeated conjuration until they obey. For some of them are sluggish, and do not willingly come among human beings, as we said above.

Secret Of The Mind

Let there be a secret of the mind which one does not choose to entrust either to a human being or to letters.

In these matters which pertain to your household affairs, money, a deposit, a loan, [unclear: adem],^6 or to any affairs whatever of human intercourse, you have a secret which you desire an absent friend far away to know; but it is of such a kind that, with the greatest danger or loss to each of you, it would come under public examination. For that reason it is to be entrusted neither to letters nor to human beings. Therefore, so that you may be secure and may fear no one’s knowledge, you turn toward the west,^7 call the duke,^8 and entrust the secret to him. He goes and faithfully carries everything through; if anything has been entrusted to him for you, he will bring it back.

Eteganographiae / Steganographiae

Letters of whatever kind you wish to write, in which you need fear no one’s inspection.

Greeting and affection. To my most beloved and most singular friend: [concerning] the bearer of the present [letter], [unclear: latior], born at Roermond,^9 very [unclear] among our friends for benefits and honors, I ask that you receive him kindly and set forth to yourself his necessity. Since he has always been joined to me by an old bond of obligation, according to my powers I would judge it very sweet to recall that [friendship] and to heap benefits upon him. And would that I could offer him consolation in his misfortunes. But since I am worn out by heavy losses, as is clearer than daylight to you, I cannot, by my own fault, do in my zeal what I would wish.

You, however, who abound in necessary temporal means, should show yourself generous and humane to a friend, just as you have shown yourself a patron of friends in necessary matters. And [my] request [is] that, by a mutual [unclear: surety/testimony], you [lend] him two hundred florins^10 for a fixed term, because the necessity set before him is very great, as [unclear: he/it] teaches. I trust that all things will be restored in full when the term appointed for him comes. If you do this, I shall give thanks that will never die, and I shall serve you in weightier matters. Act so that we may prove the sincere love shown toward us. If you do this, believe firmly that the deed will be most welcome to me, and that we shall bind him no less gratefully to you; and at the appointed term he will restore everything most completely. For it follows [unclear] to preserve promises inviolate, to provide [unclear] with these men.

Furthermore, since we were hearing joys / glad reports, I would like to write something else. I have found a little dog,^11 called by a Greek name, [unclear: refta / perhaps Recta], flourishing with such training, teaching, and memory of all things that in some respects she seems to have put off the beast and put on the human being. She understands words in Greek and Latin; she knows how to ask pardon for her faults. And, what I marvel at, she does [it], and, when I nod, immediately carries it out; she reveals human secrets. I see her equipped with such discipline of manners that I would affirm [her] a teacher to many human beings. With the windows opened, opened [again], [unclear: nature], she surpasses [others] in intelligence; when forbidden, she puts back food. Everything imposed on her she [unclear: batuit] to be shown; in zeal she is my defender, if you love me. She plays excellently and does wholly marvelous things, incredible from instruction. Farewell. Johannes Trithemius,^12 Abbot of Saint Martin in Sponheim,^13 written on the 3rd Ides of March, in the year 1500.^14

These, or any other letters whatever that he to whom it is sent will accept, he understands by the sign of the friends of the prince of the West: so that, after the customary preliminaries have been sent toward the West from the foregoing matters, he may call the spirit, attest the invisible mission, so that he may become invisible and say nothing.

Carmen Spiritus

MALGARASPRO chameron afofy mefary throes Zameda mogreal paredon adre Caphoron onaty tirno beofy. Cha-[text breaks off].^15

^1. “Malgaretic” renders OCR “Malgaretis,” likely tied to the spirit/prince name “Malgaras” immediately below. This is technical angelic/spirit nomenclature, not ordinary Latin. ^2. Clavis Steganographiae, Book I, Chapter XIII: Raysiel and the Northern Mansion

Book One

[in whatever] other [conjectured: place] or manner. You wish to [conjectured: warn] someone who does not know; but there would be great danger for you in the doing, or [unclear], if it became public. Therefore it must not be entrusted to letters, lest they be read by another, nor entrusted to a human being, lest it happen to be disclosed. So, then, that you may remain safe and your friend may be [conjectured: warned], you call a spirit,^1 entrust the secret, and it is done.

You send familiar letters to your friend, or a devout prayer, of a sort that can bear being seen.

“I had lent you my codex on the deeds of the Lombards^2 and the volume of Bede^3 on times, which I ask that you send back. For it befits a wise man, and especially a Christian, to keep everywhere the faith he has promised. To forget benefits, divine and [unclear] and human, is held to be the greatest crime. Do not incur so sinful a guilt. [Conjectured: Send back] my volumes to me, so that you may at some time [conjectured: make use of / restore] them. The Greek books, however, I gave you freely; in consideration of them you would deservedly show yourself both grateful to us and more faithful. Farewell, from Spanheim,^4 on the Ides of March,^5 in the year of the Lord 1508.”

When your friend has received these, or any other letters sent by you, and has recognized the sign of Cabariel,^6 let him turn toward that quarter of the world from which the Circius wind^7 proceeds; and, after the things customarily to be done beforehand have first been done, let him read this prayer under silence.

Song of Conjuration

Cabriel afiar paremon chiltan amedyn fayr pemadon chulcy mouayr faepor peatha mal frimafton dayr pean cothur no fabelrufyn elfoty chelmdyn.^8

When this song has been spoken facing the Circius, the angel will immediately appear visibly, disclosing to him the secret [conjectured: message]; and he reports back to you if the other has entrusted anything.

Steganography, Chapter XIII

Whose prince is called Raysiel,^9 dwelling directly toward the North, under whom are fifty princes who preside over our daytime operations,^10 and the same number over the nighttime ones; their office is to announce transmissions.^11

The thirteenth mansion is in the North. Its spirit and supreme emperor is Raysiel, who has under his dominion fifty dukes who preside over daytime operations, with many [conjectured: attendants], and the same number who preside over nighttime operations, with their servants. Their office, in these causes and transmissions that pertain to death, is to warn the friends of the operator and to announce the secret. The dukes who preside over daytime operations obey the caller freely, and they come cheerful, pleasant, and most ready to obey. But those who preside over nighttime operations are somewhat unruly, because they greatly hate and detest the light, and they do not easily obey, especially novices in the art who have been less tested; such men they very often laugh in the face, unless they are so broken by the operator’s conjurations that they cannot prevail in speaking against him. For they greatly fear conjuration, and [unclear] they are [conjectured: made / said] to be conjured more than the daytime spirits, and nevertheless they obey unwillingly. But now, from the number of all these, let us set down the names of a few and the number of their servants, as many as will be enough for our customary operation.

Baciar 50; Aflael 50; Chanael 30; Melcha 30. Thoac 50; Ranica 50; Furfiel 30; Tharas 30. Sequel 50; Dubarus 50; Bafiel 30; Vuic 30. Sadar 50; Armenia 50. Terach 50; Albhadur 50.

[unclear: Roth. S. R. S. R. S. R. S.] Thariel 40; Lasaba 40; Lamas 10; Thurcal 10. Paras 40; Alesly 40. Aryl 40; Sebah 40; Belfay 20; Sarach 20. Culmar 40; Quibda 40; Morael 20; Arepach 20.^12

You now have, excellent reader, from the fifty daytime princes, sixteen with 670 servants, and from the fifty nighttime princes, fourteen with 420 servants in number, who will suffice you for all operations both nocturnal and diurnal. But when you wish to operate through them according to the intended hours, choose from the arranged order whichever one you wish, and call him from the North, since they all dwell there, by this song.

Song of Conjuration

Ayfiel afruano chameron fosiel onear Vemabi parnothoson fruano Casfiel fuire bedarym buliffeor pean Curmaby Layr Vaymeo: pefarym adorteet odieb Vemabi peatha darfum lasphe-no deuior Camedonton phorfy lasbenay to charmon drufon olmays, Venouym luleson, peorfo faber ōtos thurno. I set down the case. There is a certain friend of mine, noble and learned, whom I know is secretly to be killed by certain hired assassins.^13 I do not dare warn [him] openly, because it is dangerous to me; in the cause [unclear: fa fa-].

Bede, probably a computistical/chronological work “on times” rather than an unspecified volume; “Vo. clumen” is an OCR split for “volumen.” ^4. The spirit-name tables are preserved as proper names with servant counts. “Roth. S. R…” appears to be damaged table/header matter, not running prose. ^13. “ficarios” is an OCR scanno for “sicarios,” assassins; “quodfdam” is recoverable as “quosdam.”

Steganographiae, Book I, Chapter XV: Armadiel

Closing Formula

“Casmeron omer vemabon.” When the song has been completed, the spirit^1 that has been sent, appearing, will faithfully carry out the office entrusted to him.

Chapter XV

Whose supreme [conjectured: emperor]^2 is Armadiel,^3 who dwells in that part of the world from which Boreas^4 is accustomed to come blowing, having under himself [conjectured: many] princes.

Armadiel, the great emperor, inhabits the fifteenth mansion^5 toward the northern quarter, having under his command many dukes and princes with their [conjectured: servitors]. Of these, one hundred have been assigned over operations by day and by night without distinction, so that they preside equally over our nocturnal and diurnal actions in Steganography^6 according to the will of the operator. Their office is to announce the operator’s most secret arcana^7 to princes and great men with the greatest fidelity and mystery. From these we shall name some of the more important, who are enough for our intention.

Example Secret

Let us fashion for ourselves, for the sake of example, such a secret as is to be entrusted to no one.

[conjectured: There is] for me, to my prince, a certain secret to be communicated to absolutely no one. I do not dare to entrust it to letters, lest through negligence or forgetfulness they be read when scattered about; much less do I wish to announce it through a human messenger, lest it happen that by him it somehow be revealed also to others. Therefore I am pleased to test the mystery of this art, through which my secret will remain hidden at all times.

Let us write letters, of whatever kind one likes, which need fear no one’s inspection.

To the most serene Prince, Lord Philip,^10 Count Palatine of the Rhine, Duke of Bavaria,^11 Archsteward of the Holy Roman Empire,^12 Prince Elector, Johannes Trithemius,^13 Abbot of Sponheim,^14 offers service with prayers.

Most illustrious Prince, with humble submission, [I offer] service. The kindness of your [conjectured: illustrious] duchy has [conjectured: instructed] me to commend to letters certain very hidden matters, set forth in words. I would rejoice, not without [conjectured: devout] exultation, if powers equal to the will were present: to assign, for the benefits shown, a most honorable and more fitting place, and to render the service owed to favor [text breaks off / OCR: “debic”].

Armadiel is the presiding name for the fifteenth northern mansion in this chapter; the name itself is not translated. ^4. Boreas is the north wind, here a directional marker for the ritual/cipher operation. ^5. “Mansio” is a station or mansion in the chapter’s directional hierarchy of operative spirits. ^6. “Steganographia” is Trithemius’s term for hidden writing/secret communication, overlaid with angelic conjuration language. ^7. “Arcana” means secrets or hidden matters; here it is both ordinary secrecy and a technical term in the steganographic setup. ^8. The conjuration is pseudo-angelic/cipher language rather than translatable Latin. Several forms are OCR-damaged; conjectures follow common positional scannos such as f/s, r/t, n/u, and c/e. ^9. “Coniuratio” is the ritual summons on the surface; in the work’s cryptographic frame it is also an operative formula. ^10. Clavis Steganographiae, Book II, Cap. IV-V: Style C Translation

Of Steganography: Closing Direction

[The sentence begins in mid-course:] ...the assigned [ones], as many as you wish, and [conjectured: entrust the secret to the more principal one].^1 Write letters in whatever form you wish, in which nothing secret is contained, and which need fear no one's inspection at all.

Letter To Rutger Vencaius

Johannes Trithemius,^2 Abbot of Spanheim, of the Order of Saint Benedict, sends greeting to Rutger Vencaius the Sicambrian,^3 canon of the order of the divine father Augustine, of the monastery of Dameten.^4

The matters that you proposed for me to solve, with Christ's help, I have resolved. Whether well, you who proposed them must render judgment. I shall briefly report to you an astonishing thing that happened. Recently a certain brother, and also a friend, not a minor one, reported to me [conjectured: that a young man had been raised from the dead at the invocation of Christ],^5 telling wonderful and [conjectured: dreadful] things among the infernal regions,^6 narrating the torments of corrupt Christians: namely, of those who crucified Christ by acting perversely; those especially guilty toward him because, forgetting the most gracious benefit of redemption,^7 they always showed themselves ungrateful to Christ; and that dreadful things are suffered by those who, by not living well, were known to be ungrateful for benefits. Blinded by sins, they neglected the joys to come and followed the pleasures of the world; with the negligences they had committed gnawing at them, they cried out most bitterly:

We deservedly endure these things, we who were always ungrateful to the redeemer of the human race; Christians in name, Gentiles in action. We miserable ones always sought earthly consolations; therefore we receive the due recompense of eternal damnation. Alas, most unhappy that we are: why did we offend Christ? Why did we despise the time granted to us?

Many other things the [conjectured: resurrected young man] reported to us, which I am now wholly unable to write, being especially hindered by weighty business. Therefore, brother, let us zealously imitate the footsteps of Christ, always giving thanks to our most gentle Savior and praying that he pardon us for the offenses committed. Farewell. 3 Kalends of April [March 30].

Reception Procedure

When the person to whom the letters are sent has received them, if he is skilled in the art, let him observe the lord of the ascendant of that same hour and the sign of the twelfth house.^8 Let him write their characters with the rest on paper, together with the other things required for the operation; then let him say the above-mentioned conjuration and, when the spirit is seen, these words: [unclear in OCR: Camerulae apropy- / apreyslertio thulinear venean maucaes fat elron; conjectured: Camerusin aproysi lierto thulnear venean maueas fabelron].^9 When these have been said, the sent spirit will approach and will faithfully and without danger reveal to him the secret entrusted to it.

Chapter V

Concerning the hour that is called Fealech, and whose supreme spirit and emperor is called [conjectured: Sasquiel; OCR Safquiel],^10 having under his command ten dukes, one hundred counts, and a very great number of servants.^11

The fifth hour of the day is called Fealech, and its spirit is named [conjectured: Sasquiel], a great and powerful emperor, who has under his command, among many, ten dukes and one hundred counts, with their attendants, appointed to the service of various and especially secret arts and of this science of ours. And it should be noted that the dukes are rarely called in the fifth hour for operations of Steganography,^12 because [conjectured: they are not always necessary], since the counts, together with the servants assigned to them, are abundantly sufficient for us in every operation.

Yet if anyone should wish to see some of the dukes as well and to make use of their power, he can call one, two, or more; and they will come without delay, since they are sufficiently benevolent and ready to obey those who operate.

[conjectured: Damiel] Iameriel Omerach - 10, 100, 1000 Araniel Futiniel Lameros - 10, 100, 1000 Maroch Rameriel Zachiel - 10, 100, 1000 Sarapiel [conjectured: Amisiel] [conjectured: Fustiel] - 10, 100, 1000 [conjectured: Putifiel] Vraniel Camiel - 10, 100, 1000

Of the dukes of [conjectured: Sasquiel] we now have the above-named; of the counts, however, ten; and from the number of servants, 5,550, whose service [conjectured: suffices for every operation of the present hour].

^1. OCR comite principaliori is a scanno for committe principaliori; v1.0's chief count is therefore wrong here. The phrase is the tail of an operation-instruction sentence. ^2. Johannes Trithemius (1462-1516), Benedictine abbot of Spanheim/Sponheim and author of the Steganographia. ^3. Rutger Vencaius Sicambro: OCR Vencio Sicambrero; this is a recoverable name/ethnic scanno, not a meaningful Latin form. ^4. Coenobium Dametense: OCR Conobij Dametenfis. Place/institutional identification remains authorially obscure beyond the Latin title as printed. ^5. The clause resuscitatum fuisse iuvenem... ex mortuis is heavily damaged in OCR as reficitur tamen fusificium... ex mortis; this is a recoverable scanno cluster, not intelligible Latin. Recovery checked against the same-passage transcription at https://www.esotericarchives.com/tritheim/steg4.htm. ^6. inferi/inferos: Christian infernal regions or hell in this moral exemplum, not merely the neutral classical underworld. ^7. redemptionis beneficium: theological term for Christ's saving work; the OCR has redemptionis beneficium fairly visible but surrounding syntax is damaged. ^8. lord of the ascendant and twelfth house: technical astrological terms used in the ritualized operating procedure. ^9. characteres and coniuratio are technical terms: written astrological/ritual signs and the conjuration formula. The Camerusin formula is occult vocabulary, not a German tenor; OCR corrupts and splits it across the page break. ^10. Sasquiel: OCR repeatedly gives Safquiel. The s/f confusion is a common early-print/OCR scanno; the same chapter's catalog supports Sasquiel. ^11. duces, comites, servi: hierarchy titles in the spirit catalog; translate literally as dukes, counts, servants, but they are technical ranks rather than ordinary military offices. ^12. Steganographia: here both Trithemius's work and the claimed hidden-message art; do not flatten it into generic cryptography.

Style C Translation: Steganographiae, Liber Secundus, pp. 123-124

Steganographia

[It] is sufficient for every operation of the present hour. Therefore, when you wish to operate in steganography^1 through any one of the aforesaid [spirits] in the fifth hour of the day,^2 write the character^3 of the lord of the ascendant,^4 of the twelfth house,^5 together with the other things required for the art, on a clean slip of paper; and on its back [write] this conjuration, in the same manner as you have done [before].

Conjuration

Saequi adres raetrofeti rofiei emelto satu olmeniel irfoti faucar nauediel liernoti chamefon.^6

When these things have been completed, and the other necessary matters joined to them, say this very conjuration as is proper; and immediately you will see the spirit whom you have called visibly present. To him you may safely entrust the secret.

Method for Announcing a Secret

If we have some secret, of whatever kind, for a friend, which we wish no one except him to know, and if it is of such a kind that it may safely be entrusted neither to letters nor to messengers,^7 let us call one of the companions of the aforesaid Saequiel;^8 let us entrust the secret to him; let us add letters sealed with his character; and surely we shall [unclear].

Tenor of the Letter, at Pleasure

Johannes Trithemius,^9 abbot of Spanheim,^10 to the religious brother Nicolaus Baefius of Dureckheim,^11 monk of Hirsau,^12 greeting.

[unclear: Saequitam] obedience, good brother, and humility you deny us; blessed constitutions [have been] [unclear: laefactas]. By the report of all, [unclear] joined, known, that you have hatred for good zeal; [unclear] to preserve the religious rule and Catholic obedience; to be occupied rather proudly with secular arts. Good brother, what are you doing? You are zealous for troublesome and foolish double-tongued men; you love hatred, bitterness, quarrels, and disputes; you hate goodness; you are double-tongued, contentious, proud.

Fool, what are you doing? It is time, all the more quickly, according to justice, [conjectured: to correct] these negligences of yours and the zeal of bitterness with the scourges of humility; and [unclear] you are compelled humbly to break off your cares for us [unclear] by office to be zealous against all things which [unclear] in the acts of your faith and in Catholic morals [unclear: of sedition]. Farewell from Spanheim, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the year 1500.^13

When the person to whom the letter is sent has received it, if he is skilled in the art and has recognized the character of Safquiel [probably Saequiel],^14 and after the customary preliminaries have first been performed, let him say the above-mentioned conjuration; and immediately the spirit sent will appear and show himself visibly. When he has seen him, let him at once say these words:

Fabelmerusyn aueal vear plyn an cralti penafon.^15

When the spirit has heard these words spoken, he will at once approach and reveal the secret.

Chapter VI

Whose hour is called Genapherym,^16 and whose spirit, a supreme emperor, is called Saniel,^17 who has under him 110 dukes and counts, with many servants.

The sixth hour of the day is called Genapherym, and the angel to whom it belongs is Saniel, great and powerful in visible operations. He has under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts, and 5,500 servants assigned to the service of diverse operations; these are sufficient for us for all things that we may wish to perform through steganography in this hour.

The dukes, however, are called more rarely, although they are prompt and very willing to obey our commands, because their counts have generally been accustomed to carry out their offices, since they themselves are often occupied in other magical experiments.^18

Arnebiel 10; Charuch 10; Medieliel 10; Nathmiel 10; Pemiel 10; Gamuel 100; Ienoriel 100; Samcon 100; Trafzel 100; Xamyon 100; Nedabar 100; Permon 100; Brasil 100; Camofiel 100; Euadur 100.^19

^1. “Steganographia” is both the title and Trithemius’s technical term for concealed writing; here it is embedded in an angelic-ritual frame. ^2. “quinta hora diei”: the fifth planetary/ritual hour of the day, continuing the previous chapter’s hour-system. ^3. “characterem”: a magical or cipher-sign used to identify and authorize the spirit; not merely a written letter. ^4. “domini ascendentes” is OCR-damaged for “domini ascendentis,” the astrological lord of the ascendant. ^5. “domus duodecimae”: the twelfth astrological house; the syntax is compressed but recoverable. ^6. Barbarous conjuration formula. I preserve the OCR text rather than normalize the spirit-names; “chamefon” may reflect long-s/f confusion or type damage. ^7. “tabellionibus” strictly means notaries/scribes, but in this practical context probably means entrusted carriers or letter-handlers; I avoid over-certainty. ^8. “Saequiaelis / Saequielis”: OCR and orthographic variation in the name of the fifth-hour spirit or its ruler. ^9. Johannes Trithemius, Benedictine abbot and author of the Steganographia. ^10. Spanheim/Sponheim, Trithemius’s abbey; the print has “Spanheimensis” and later abbreviated “Spanh.” ^11. Nicolaus Baefius of Dureckheim: named recipient in the sample letter; spelling may be affected by OCR and early-modern orthography. ^12. Hirsau, Benedictine monastery; “Hirsaugieni” is an OCR/inflectional form for Hirsaugiensi. ^13. “prid. Cal. April.” = pridie Kalendas Aprilis, March 31. “Anno M.D.” = 1500. ^14. “Safquielis” is likely OCR for “Saequielis”; f/long-s and q/e confusions are common in this material. ^15. Second barbarous formula, apparently an operative command for disclosure of the entrusted secret; no German plaintext is visible in this excerpt. ^16. “Genapherym”: name of the sixth hour; preserved as printed. ^17. Saniel: angel/spirit governing the sixth hour in this chapter. ^18. “magici” here modifies “experiments” in the ritual-magic sense; the passage presents a magical hierarchy of officers. ^19. The list is a register of subordinate spirits and their assigned numbers. The page layout marks some rows with “R.” and “T.”; their function is not recoverable from this excerpt alone.

STEGANOGRAPHIAE / Liber Secundus, Cap. VII

Steganographiae

We have here named from the dukes of Samiel^1: from the counts, 10; and from the number of the servants, 550, through whom the operation of steganography^2 is performed in the sixth hour of the day.^3 Therefore, when you wish to operate through those spirits, keep yourself wholly in a secret place; and if you wish to call one duke or several, let that be in your power, although there is no need, because the counts will suffice for making everything known to us. Therefore write on a clean little sheet^4 the customary characters of the planets and signs,^5 and on its back the conjuration.

Conjuration

Samiel asiel thebream pothijr erfory mear pornys layr moas, famerofyn.^6 Then, once the preliminaries have first been performed, say the same conjuration in the rite by which it [unclear: is known / is done]; and immediately the spirit called will be present, ready and eager for all things; you may send him far or near to a friend, so that he may carry the secret.

Argument of the Secret

Whatever secret you have, to whomever [you wish], you can send it securely, being more expert in the art of steganography, through the spirits of Samiel in the sixth hour of the day; for they are general agents for making all things known and altogether faithful in commissions,^7 if you proceed in all things in the due manner according to our precepts.

Form of the Letters, as You Please

H[unclear]. With very humble laments, praying, we shall obtain the grace of remission by groans; and the things that are received [bring?] freedom from guilt. Let people who are continually penitent receive [unclear: gladness/latitude] by merit; justice, by works adorned with Catholic piety, [unclear] to the law of kindness, and praise comes to the Catholic [Church/faith]. The most merciful savior will free all, and, sins having been remitted, those desiring pardon, those loving [unclear], passing over, will receive the joys of Catholic religion and of blessedness. Good [unclear: powers/possessions?], for the liberated, [unclear: passing over] for those keeping the law, will obtain the bright blessedness of the glory of the triumphant in the light of the Trinity.^8 In the year 1500, on the Kalends of April.^9 Joan. Tris. Abb. wrote [this].^10

Liber Secundus

When the person to whom these letters are sent has received them, being skilled in the art, after the preliminaries have first been performed, let him say the conjuration; and soon the spirit sent will appear. When he sees him present, let him say these words:

Charmes pormeniel vear faenui liernoty noty erfy melron.^11

After these have been said, as is prescribed in the art, the spirit will draw nearer and will faithfully and secretly reveal the secret committed to him.

Cap. VII

Of the hour which is called Hamarym,^12 and its spirit Barquiel,^13 having under his command 10 dukes, 100 counts. The number of servants is not certain to me.

The seventh hour of the day is called Hamarym, and its angel is called Barquiel; he has under his command 100 dukes and 100 counts. The number of servants is great and uncertain. The ministries of all these, by their turns and in their own orders, are abundantly sufficient for us for every operation of steganography in the seventh hour of the day. But when you wish to operate through the spirits of the aforesaid emperor in the seventh hour, do not call fewer than at least one duke and one count, who have servants assigned to them, each in his own order. But so that you may have at hand the names of some dukes and counts through whom you seek to operate, attend to the table.

N[ames?].

Abrasiel; Farmos; Nefiorii [or Nestorii?]; Manuel; Sagiel; Harmiel; Nafrus; Varmay; Tulmas; Crofiel; Pafriel; Venfciel [conjectured: Vensciel/Venfriel?]; Enarym; Drufcel; Kathos.

10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 10 10 10 10 10 / 100 100 100 100 100.

Here [unclear: now you have] named from the dukes, 5; from the counts, 10; and [the text breaks off].

^1. Samielis is the governing spirit/angel-name for the sixth hour in this section; spelling is not normalized to Samael, since the OCR/source reads Samielis here. ^2. Steganographia is Trithemius’s technical term for concealed writing under angelic-spirit fiction; translated as “steganography” but left conceptually tied to the work’s cipher art. ^3. “Sixth hour of the day” is a ritual/cipher scheduling term in this chapter, not ordinary clock-time alone. ^4. Chartula mundo is almost certainly chartula munda, “clean little sheet”; OCR has mundo for munda or an inflectional/scanno error. ^5. “Characters of the planets and signs” refers to astrological/magical signs used as operational cover or apparatus in the Steganographia. ^6. The conjuration words are not Latin and are preserved as printed/OCR’d; pothijr may reflect early-modern i/j interchange or OCR uncertainty. ^7. “in commulis” is likely in commissis, “in commissions/entrusted matters”; OCR confuses ss/long-s clusters and may have read commissis poorly. ^8. This pious “letter form” is syntactically strained and contains many OCR scannos: Vnúlimis likely humillimis/humilimis; affidue = assidue; iniftitia = iustitia; poifimus = piissimus; remiftique = remissisque; tranfite/tranfitem and fervantibus reflect long-s/f confusion. I have not silently repaired all Latin because the cover text may be cipher-bearing. ^9. “M.D. Cal. Apr.” = 1500, Kalends of April, i.e. April 1, 1500, if read in the ordinary Roman-calendar sense. ^10. “Joan. Tris. Abb.” abbreviates Johannes Trithemius, Abbot; the final scriptit is non-classical/erroneous for scripsit or a printed/OCR form. ^11. Second formula is also non-Latin cipher/angelic diction and is preserved. “His dicitis” is likely his dictis, “when these have been said”; “acceder” likely accedet. ^12. Hamarym is the name assigned to the seventh hour; preserved as a technical spirit-hour name. ^13. Barquiel is the angel/spirit of the seventh hour in this passage; the chapter heading says 10 dukes, but the body reads 100 dukes, a source inconsistency not harmonized here.

Clavis Steganographiae, Book II: Tartys and the Sample Letter to the Nuns of Mount St Rupert

Book Two

Here we have six named from the dukes of Tartys,^1 and twelve from the counts; likewise 1,320 servants,^2 numbered and distributed by turns and ranks, who will suffice us at this hour for the experiment of the art.^3

And note that, according to Solomon^4 and Raziel,^5 all those dukes and princes of Tartys are benevolent and most ready for obedience; and in whatever form they have been ordered to appear, they willingly assume it. Therefore, when you wish to operate in this science,^6 observe diligently the lord of the ascendant,^7 together with the other things that we prescribe, and write everything that is to be written with this conjuration.

Conjuration

Tartys chrybes faziel yrstci haelnot dreor aduear afy mearo Veny satu pemertson.

Then, when all things have been completed most diligently, and the conjuration has been read in due manner, as is proper, the spirits that have been called will presently be there, ready for your command.

Let the secret, whatever occurs to us, be great and difficult.

The secret that we wish to [conjectured: intimate / make known] to a friend through the spirits may be whatever occurs to us according to the time and the variety of affairs, provided that it is not trifling, and not of such a kind that it can be reported safely by other means.

Cover Letter

Johannes Trithemius^8 to the nuns^9 on Mount Saint Rupert,^10 who adorn the Catholic faith with bright virginity: [may they] continually merit eternal happiness by the most holy zeal of religion.

By the mercy of the Eternal King^11 we prudently send to you the man long expected, a man of great experience in temporal matters, Johannes, born of Raunenstat,^12 the reverend and zealous abbot for a long time of the monastery of [conjectured: Vosldorf],^13 and now freely [conjectured: resigning] that same abbacy. On account of him there is added, as I had promised you, the monk of Limburg,^14 in whom Christ [unclear], occupied with continual prayers and with holy readings of the Scriptures, together with the monks of the same monastery; and you ask that he be sent to your convent,^15 and that he take up care of temporal affairs, and become procurator^16 and cellarer.^17 The abbot of Limburg, in his accustomed [unclear], changed in mind, was able to admit him once consent had been obtained from him. At last, with Christ [conjectured: breathing into / prompting him], he consented, though fearfully, for this reason: because he fears he will be [conjectured: struck / wounded] by nuns, who are very lightly changed. He does not fear undeservedly, since experience has taught us thus: at times nuns have repaid their stewards,^18 for benefits, with a reward not praiseworthy. A feminine mind is suddenly changed by a zeal of bitterness. But, with Christ granting it, let him be thus with you. He is a Christian, he is a monk, he fears [conjectured: for salvation / salutary things], and he is of good understanding. Therefore accustom yourselves to restrain womanly instability, so that you may remember to be constant: [conjectured: receiving] him with holy honor and sincere charity, laying aside all lightness of womanly spirit, especially since you are able, with the aid of Christ the Redeemer, to help him and to receive [conjectured: the restoration] of the temporal affairs of your monastery, which have collapsed, [unclear: who / which] [conjectured: has zealously loved] charity. Farewell. From Sponheim,^19 on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May,^20 in the year of our Lord Jesus Christ 1500.

Instruction After The Letter

When the person to whom they are sent has received letters marked with the character of Tartys,^21 being skilled in our art, let him observe the lord of the ascendant and do, most diligently, each and every thing that is to be done, and let him append the usual conjuration. And when he has seen that many spirits are present, let him say these words to the principal one:

Chabor maflotiel tu[e]uo reneas porean trismeny penarfon.

And when he has said these words with strong intention to the principal duke, immediately, approaching peaceably, he will reveal the secret.

^1. Tartys is the named spirit-region or hierarchy in this section. OCR has “exducibus” for “ex ducibus”; this is a spacing/scanno issue, not a lexical variant. ^2. “servants” translates servi; OCR “feruos” reflects long-s/s and u/v confusion. ^3. “art” is the steganographic-magical procedure of the Clavis/Steganographia, not a fine art. ^4. Solomon is invoked as an authority for spirit-conjuration literature; no attempt is made here to identify a specific Solomonic text. ^5. Raziel: OCR “Ratielem” is likely a scanno for “Razielem,” the angel/textual authority known from Razielic magical tradition. ^6. “science” translates scientia, here a learned technical art or discipline. ^7. “lord of the ascendant” is astrological vocabulary: the planet ruling the zodiacal sign rising at the operation’s chosen time. OCR “dominum ascendens” is best read as “dominum ascendentis.” ^8. Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim and author/compiler of the Steganographia tradition. ^9. Sanctimoniales: professed religious women, here rendered “nuns.” ^10. Mount Saint Rupert: “monte Almi Ruperti”; the place-name is clear despite OCR damage in surrounding text. ^11. “Eternal King” translates Aeterni Regis; OCR splits this as “A Terni Regis.” ^12. Raunenstat: personal/place byname as printed/OCR’d; identification uncertain from this passage alone. ^13. “Vosldorf” is damaged: OCR “Vosldorpensif” probably stands for a monastic adjective in -ensis. The exact house-name is not securely recoverable from the supplied text. ^14. Limburg: OCR “Lympurgen-tem” likely represents “Lympurgensem/Limburgensem,” a monk of Limburg. ^15. “convent” translates coenobium; OCR “canobium” is a common ae/e scanno. ^16. Procurator: monastic officer or business manager handling external/temporal affairs. ^17. Cellarer: monastic officer responsible for stores and provisions. ^18. Oeconomici: household/estate managers or stewards; the passage complains about nuns repaying such managers badly. ^19. Sponheim: “Spanh.” is the usual abbreviated origin for Trithemius’s abbey context. ^20. Seventeenth day before the Kalends of May is April 15 by inclusive Roman reckoning. ^21. “character of Tartys” means the graphic sign/sigil or written cipher-character belonging to this spirit hierarchy; it is both magical and cryptographic vocabulary here.

Style C Translation: Steganographiae 134-135

Steganographiae, p. 134

For in the first order there are 10; in the second 20; in the third 30; in the fourth 40; in the fifth 50; in the sixth 60; in the seventh 70; in the eighth 80; in the ninth 90; in the tenth 100; in the eleventh 1,000; in the twelfth 10,000. And from these twelve orders, in their proper turns, spirits^1 are sent to us for service in the operations of the art of Steganography^2; of these we now name others.

R. Armofiel, Rayziel, Lamediel: 10, 100, 100, 1000
R. Nedruan, Gemezin, Adroziel: 10, 100, 100, 1000
R. Maneylor, Fremiel, Zodiel: 10, 100, 100, 1000
R. Ormael, Hamay, Bramiel: 10, 100, 100, 1000
R. Phorsiel, Iapuriel, Coreziel: 10, 100, 100, 1000
R. Rimexyn, Ispfiel, Enatriel: 10, 100, 100, 1000

Here we have, from the spirit Iesicha^3, six leaders and twelve companions named, to whom are assigned ministering spirits^4 [conjectured: 7,260]. These, in their turns and orders, are sent into the service of the person operating in the art. The princes themselves, according to the saying of Solomon the Philosopher^5, are manifold in form; and whatever forms they are ordered to take, they will assume. Therefore, when you wish to operate through them in the fourth hour of the night^6, observe the ascending house^7 and [conjectured: the whole] figure of the sky, and do everything according to what [conjectured: you have been instructed]; striking/writing all things on a clean sheet^8, and on its back this conjuration^9.

Conjuration

Iesicha ofiel mear pathyr lays mean theor dreochifis zan moabl lofeas erstsi breo pornys tayr penarfon.

Then, after [unclear] have been [unclear], when you have said that conjuration itself in due manner, form, and order, the spirits will appear visibly in whatever form you have commanded, ready and willing for all things.

The Secret Is Made at Will

Whatever secret occurs to you for the occasion, which you wish an absent person to know at this fourth hour of the night, you may entrust it securely to the spirits, provided it is such that it cannot safely be communicated to him either by letters or by messengers. For those things which we can communicate without danger either by letters or by messengers, we ought by no means to communicate through the ministry of spirits. But whoever shall presume to call upon spirits for light and secret matters which can be communicated without danger by letters or messengers will without doubt bring back loss and inconvenience, with danger.

Wording of the Letter at Will

To the venerable father in Christ, the steward^10 of the Limburgers, the religious lord called Ioannes Weisvorsen^11, Ioannes Oulis,^12 humble abbot of Spanheim,^13 [conjectured: the joys of heaven].

The nuns of Saint Rupert^14 [unclear: desire/choose] you as their governor with excessive [unclear], and ask you with humble goodwill that, [unclear] the times of affairs, you undertake the governance of that monastery. To serve the [conjectured: devout] virgins of Christ is praiseworthy and [unclear] a good of spiritual things. [The text then presents you/the named man as] visitor of that same named and renowned convent, filling you with the greatest honor: weighty in morals, adorned with virtues, cautious in counsel, loved by all, of good reputation among religious persons for monastic conduct, and notable to holy men; whose life, by the merit of Christ, is very pleasing; the excellent abbot of the monastery of Saint John.^15 In the letters of both Christians and gentiles he is most learned and most trustworthy, and is very learned; he notably surpasses the wisdom of [unclear: ordinary/fortunate?] men. He knows very well how to rule the flock entrusted to him. And he has zeal for the causes of the virgins of Christ, whose cloister he preserves most firmly. Do not fear to serve under him among such good nuns, for he knows how to govern the brides of Christ according to monastic law with excellent discretion; by virtue and zeal for the Christian faith he will freely assist you in necessity. Gladly accept this man, so distinguished and kindly, as pastor and familiar [conjectured: guardian] for the governance of such religious virgins. Christ [unclear] eternal joy[s] [breaks off].

^1. “Spirits” here belongs to Trithemius’s pseudo-angelic / demonic operative vocabulary in the Steganographia, not to ordinary Christian pneumatology alone. ^2. Steganographia: Trithemius’s art of concealed writing, presented in ritual-magical language. ^3. Iesicha is a spirit-name in the passage. The form may be affected by OCR at the initial letter, but the conjuration below also gives “Iesicha,” so I have not normalized it silently. ^4. “Ministering spirits” translates ministeriales; the figure “72. 60.” is damaged/ambiguous. It may intend 7,260 rather than “72 and 60.” ^5. Solomon the Philosopher: conventional authority-name in magical and pseudo-Solomonic traditions; not a recoverable historical citation here. ^6. Fourth hour of the night: a technical timing instruction for the operation. ^7. “Ascending house” is astrological vocabulary: the domus ascendens, linked to the ascendant. ^8. schedula munda is defensibly “a clean sheet/slip.” OCR has “mudam” for mundam; this is a typical n/m/u scanno in damaged early print OCR. ^9. Conjuration: ritual formula; the barbarous-language string is not translated and should not be regularized. ^10. Oeconomus: steward/administrator, probably an ecclesiastical office in context. ^11. Ioannes Weisvorsen: personal name left as transmitted; spelling may be OCR-damaged. ^12. Ioannes Oulis is likely OCR-damaged for Johannes Trithemius’s name/title formula, but “Oulis” is not safely reconstructable from the provided text. ^13. Spanheimensis Abbas: abbot of Sponheim/Spanheim, Trithemius’s office. ^14. Saint Rupert: likely the monastery of St. Rupert near Bingen, associated with the nuns in this letter-context. ^15. Monastery of Saint John: named institution in the damaged encomium; exact referent is not reconstructed from this OCR alone.

MODVS PRIMVS OCCVLTE scribendi

Heading

The first method^1 of writing secretly is made by the several first letters of individual words; its sign is this: I.

Preface to the Method

[Conjectured: The first, therefore, method] of writing secretly is as follows. When you wish to write something secretly to a friend, so that no one should understand your intention except the person to whom you write, then [conjectured: take] whatever Latin narrative you wish, [unclear], placing every [conjectured: word] in order, so that the first letter of each [conjectured: word] may render, freely, the word that you wish, as I shall teach you in the argument or example set below. But this method is not sufficiently [conjectured: safe for the future], because it could easily be detected by an industrious person, as will now be [conjectured: tried/shown]. In reading it is indeed easy; but it is written with difficulty, because it is laborious always to have at hand [conjectured: words] suited to the proposed thing. Now let us set down an example of this method: the open text^2 is Latin, but the tenor^3 [conjectured: of the secret] is found written in German,^4 namely:

The third method is to use alternate words in such a way that the first is always empty of the secret meaning.
